Daily News

Science · Technology

Physicists listened to electrical noise to crack a superconductor mystery

Global · Notable · New

Briefing produced 09 Nov 2026, 3:00 AM NZDT

Physicists used shot noise measurements to show that electron pairing in cuprate superconductors occurs at the pseudogap energy, supporting the theory that pre-formed pairs exist before superconductivity. The study, published in Science, found that pairing is associated with the pseudogap, ruling out the hypothesis that it arises solely from frozen electron patterns, though it does not exclude intertwined mechanisms.

Why it matters

The findings suggest that the bottleneck for higher-temperature superconductivity in cuprates is achieving phase coherence among pre-formed pairs, rather than forming the pairs themselves, which could guide future material design efforts.

Briefing produced 09 Nov 2026, 3:00 AM NZDT

The strikes occurred on Monday, just before US midterm elections, while mediators from Qatar and Pakistan facilitated negotiations to prevent a return to all-out war. Iranian negotiators had previously proposed reopening the strait within two days if the US met seven conditions, including lifting a naval blockade and releasing frozen assets.

Why it matters

Its effective closure due to the conflict and US naval blockade has disrupted commercial shipping, prompting US military protection for tankers and intense diplomatic efforts to restore stability.

The Bantu expansion changed Africa. Scientists are still tracing how.

Briefing produced 09 Nov 2026, 3:00 AM NZDT

Scientists are reconstructing the Bantu expansion, a migration from western Africa starting 6,000 to 4,000 years ago that introduced farming and metalworking to sub-Saharan Africa. A 2024 genomic analysis of 1,763 Africans found the greatest genetic diversity among Bantu speakers in western Africa, supporting a population expansion from that region. Archaeological evidence, including pottery in the Congo rainforest dating to 2,300–2,000 years ago, suggests Bantu groups crossed the forest together before splitting into east- and south-moving groups 2,500 to 3,500 years ago.

Why it matters

The expansion reshaped sub-Saharan Africa's demography, introducing sedentary lifestyles and metalworking to hunter-gatherer regions. Today, approximately 350 million Africans speak Bantu languages, and many carry Bantu ancestry, making this one of history's largest human migrations.

WHO urged to review nitrate drinking water limit

Global · NZ · Notable · Catch up

Briefing produced 09 Nov 2026, 3:00 AM NZDT

Over 80 international organizations, including New Zealand groups, signed a letter urging the WHO to review its nitrate drinking water limit, which has remained unchanged since 1958. Signatories argue the current guideline fails to reflect recent evidence linking chronic low-level nitrate exposure to health risks such as colorectal cancer and pre-term birth. The letter requests a full evaluation of nitrate as a chemical contaminant and a review of epidemiological evidence.

Why it matters

New Zealand's drinking water standard aligns with the WHO guideline, and a review could influence national water safety policies. A Ministry of Health review of nitrate health effects is expected to be completed by the end of the year.

Arizona State University researchers identified an epigenetic mechanism explaining why large dogs age faster than small ones, finding that giant breeds lose roughly 35 percent more LINE1 DNA methylation annually than small breeds. This reduced regulation of "jumping genes" is linked to increased DNA damage and age-related diseases. The study, published in Science, used data from 864 dogs to map these methylation patterns across the genome.

Why it matters

The findings provide a clear molecular signature for the size-lifespan trade-off in dogs, offering a valuable model for biologists to study aging mechanisms in other mammals.

RNZ Business published reader questions regarding personal finance, including a 57-year-old seeking to use KiwiSaver for private hip surgery and a 70-year-old asking about selling a rental property. Experts explained that KiwiSaver hardship withdrawals are unavailable if a mortgage top-up is possible, as the scheme is designed for retirement. Why it matters

The responses clarify the strict limitations of KiwiSaver access for medical costs and provide specific strategies for older New Zealanders to manage asset-rich, cash-poor financial situations.
